raw_case_text:
A 52-year-old male presented with dull, aching pain in the right hypochondriac region that radiated toward the left hypochondrium for four months. The patient also had breathlessness, cough, and intermittent fever, which was associated with nausea, vomiting, and weight loss. The patient was a shepherd by occupation and had regular contact with livestock and dogs. The patient had been on medical treatment for jaundice for the past five months, but there was no previous documentation available with him. The patient had a poorly built physique and was moderately nourished in appearance. The patient exhibited pallor and mild icterus, with no signs of cyanosis, clubbing, or lymphadenopathy. Vital signs upon admission were as follows: a pulse rate of 122/min, blood pressure of 100/70 mmHg, and oxygen saturation levels of 90% on room air. Physical examination revealed a soft and tender abdomen on the right. The left hypochondrium revealed no guarding, rigidity, distension, or palpable mass. Hepatosplenomegaly was observed on further examination. Auscultation revealed decreased air entry over the right side of the chest and normal air entry over the left side of the chest. The computed tomography (CT) report was suggestive of a hydatid cyst in the right lung (Figure 1).
The abdominal CT indicated the presence of large, well-defined multi-loculated cystic lesions in the right lung, along with multi-loculated lesions in the segments of the liver. These liver lesions showed septations and tiny foci of calcifications, suggesting hydatid cysts in the liver, spleen, and lung (Figures 2-4).
A lesion causing a mass effect, manifested as the compression of intrahepatic biliary radicals and prominence of inter-hepatic biliary radicals along with the common bile duct, was indicative of hepatomegaly, with the liver measuring 19.2 cm. The spleen size was noted to be 14 cm, displaying a similarly large, well-defined cystic lesion in the splenic parenchyma with multiple foci and the presence of daughter cysts. These findings lead to the conclusion that the reports suggest hydatid cysts of the spleen. Based on these findings, hydatid cysts of the liver, lung, and spleen were confirmed. The patients' laboratory investigation profile is presented in Table 1.
Case management
Preoperatively, the patient was transfused with two units of packed red blood cells (PRBCs), one unit of whole blood, and three units of platelets. Increased creatinine levels were managed through hydration over the course of several days, and urinary output was monitored based on the guidance provided by the nephrologists. The patient was administered antibiotics for two weeks before surgery, and prophylactic therapy with albendazole was started immediately after the diagnosis. Surgery was planned after obtaining fitness clearance from the anesthesia and medicine teams. The operative management involved a right thoracotomy and an approach to extract the hydatid cyst of the lung without any spillage, a procedure that was successfully completed. A right subcostal incision was made to extract the hydatid cyst in the liver. All daughter cysts were extracted with due precautions, with no spillage in the peritoneal cavity. A left subcostal incision was made to extract hydatid cysts of the spleen, and marsupialization of splenic hydatid cysts was completed (Figure 5).
The contents inside the cavity were scraped off, and marsupialization of the splenic hydatid cyst was performed. This was followed by washing the peritoneal cavity with a cetrimide solution and subsequent cleaning with hypertonic saline. Hemostasis was achieved. The abdominal layers were closed, and the skin was sutured. The postoperative period was uneventful, and the patient had no complaints other than mild pain at the incision site. Albendazole treatment was continued. The samples were sent for histopathology, and the report confirmed a hydatid cyst of the liver and spleen.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 52-year-old male shepherd presented with a 4-month history of dull right hypochondriac pain radiating to the left hypochondrium, accompanied by breathlessness, cough, intermittent fever, nausea, vomiting, and weight loss.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient experienced dull, aching right hypochondriac pain radiating to the left hypochondrium for 4 months, associated with dyspnea, cough, intermittent fever, nausea, vomiting, and weight loss. He had been receiving undocumented medical treatment for jaundice for the preceding 5 months.
subjective.past_medical_history: Medical treatment for jaundice for 5 months. Worked as a shepherd with regular contact with livestock and dogs.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for right-to-left hypochondriac pain, dyspnea, cough, intermittent fever, nausea, vomiting, jaundice, and weight loss.

objective.physical_examination: Poorly built, moderately nourished male with pallor and mild icterus; no cyanosis, clubbing, or lymphadenopathy. Vital signs: pulse 122/min, blood pressure 100/70 mmHg, and SpO2 90% on room air. Chest auscultation revealed decreased air entry on the right side. Abdominal examination showed right-sided tenderness and hepatosplenomegaly without left hypochondriac guarding, rigidity, or distension.
objective.routine_investigations: Preoperative laboratory workup showed anemia, thrombocytopenia, and elevated serum creatinine requiring transfusion of 2 units PRBCs, 1 unit whole blood, 3 units platelets, and intravenous hydration.
objective.advanced_workup: Thoracic and abdominal CT revealed a large, well-defined multiloculated cystic lesion in the right lung, hepatomegaly (19.2 cm) with multiloculated septated and focally calcified cystic lesions compressing the intrahepatic biliary radicles and common bile duct, and splenomegaly (14 cm) with a large multiloculated cystic lesion containing daughter cysts. Histopathology of the excised surgical specimens confirmed hydatid cysts of the liver and spleen.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Disseminated cystic echinococcosis involving the right lung, liver, and spleen, confirmed by characteristic multiloculated daughter-cyst CT findings and postoperative histopathology. After preoperative stabilization (blood/platelet transfusions, IV hydration for renal dysfunction, 2 weeks of antibiotics, and prophylactic albendazole), the patient underwent right thoracotomy for intact extraction of the pulmonary hydatid cyst, right subcostal laparotomy for extraction of hepatic daughter cysts, and left subcostal incision for splenic hydatid marsupialization with cetrimide and hypertonic saline peritoneal lavage; he recovered uneventfully and continued postoperative albendazole.
